title: Where I live
goal: Describe your home — and put in place the third form of the article, the **Dativ**, which you use every time you say where something is.
bekal: say what's in a place (*Es gibt…*)
say where things are with the Dativ (*in der Küche*)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Die neue Wohnung
dialogs.intro: Lena is visiting Budi's apartment for the first time. A conversation like this is almost entirely about places — and places mean the Dativ.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Oh, die Wohnung ist schön! Wie viele Zimmer hast du?
lines.id: Oh, the apartment is lovely! How many rooms do you have?
lines.literal: oh, the apartment is beautiful! how many rooms have you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zwei. Es gibt ein Schlafzimmer und ein Wohnzimmer.
lines.id: Two. There's a bedroom and a living room.
lines.literal: two. it gives a sleep-room and a living-room.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und die Küche? Ist sie groß?
lines.id: And the kitchen? Is it big?
lines.literal: and the kitchen? is she big?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nein, ziemlich klein. Aber es gibt einen Balkon.
lines.id: No, fairly small. But there's a balcony.
lines.literal: no, rather small. but it gives a balcony.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Next to the kitchen, at the back on the right.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: And what's in the living room?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ein Sofa, ein Tisch und ein Regal. Der Fernseher steht auf dem Regal.
lines.id: A sofa, a table and a shelf. The TV is on the shelf.
lines.literal: a sofa, a table and a shelf. the TV-set stands on the shelf.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und wo schläfst du? Auf dem Sofa?
lines.id: And where do you sleep? On the sofa?
lines.literal: and where sleep you? on the sofa?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nein! Mein Bett steht im Schlafzimmer, natürlich.
lines.id: No! My bed is in the bedroom, of course.
lines.literal: no! my bed stands in-the sleep-room, naturally.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sechshundert Euro warm. Das ist günstig für Berlin.
lines.id: Six hundred euros, heating included. That's cheap for Berlin.
lines.literal: six-hundred euro warm. that is cheap for Berlin.

notes: ***Es gibt* is always followed by the Akkusativ.** Look at line 4: *es gibt **einen** Balkon*. Literally "it gives a balcony", and the item really is the object of "giving". The form never changes — it's never *es geben*, even with a plural: *Es gibt zwei Zimmer.*

**Places take the Dativ.** *in **der** Küche*, *auf **dem** Regal*, *neben **der** Küche*. This third form of the article appears every time you answer the question *wo?* — which means it appears constantly.

***stehen*, *liegen*, *hängen* — not *sein*.** Germans describe exactly how an object is positioned: upright things *stehen* (a table, a bottle, a wardrobe), flat things *liegen* (a book on a table, a towel), hanging things *hängen* (a picture, a jacket). *Der Fernseher **steht** auf dem Regal* sounds far more natural than *ist*.

**Lines 7 and 10: *im* = *in dem*.** German merges prepositions with the Dativ article: *in dem → **im***, *an dem → **am***, *bei dem → **beim***, *zu dem → **zum***, *zu der → **zur***. These contractions are standard, not optional — *in dem Wohnzimmer* sounds odd unless you're stressing one particular room.

***Warm* and *kalt* in rental talk** have nothing to do with temperature: *Warmmiete* is rent including heating and water, *Kaltmiete* is the bare rent. The difference can be a hundred euros or more, so the first question about any apartment ad is always *warm oder kalt?*
***Wie hoch ist die Miete?*** is literally "how high is the rent" — in German, rents, salaries and taxes are *hoch* or *niedrig*, not *teuer* or *billig*. Only things you buy are *teuer*.

grammars.title: The Dativ: the third form of the article
body: You've already used the Nominativ (the subject) and the Akkusativ (the object). The third form, the **Dativ**, does two jobs at A1: saying **where** something is, and following a certain group of prepositions.
after: A helpful pattern: in the Dativ, masculine and neuter are **always the same** (*dem*), and feminine uses what was the masculine Nominativ form (*der*). ⚠️ So *der* can mean two things — *der Mann* (masculine Nominativ) and *der Frau* (feminine Dativ). Context decides.
The Dativ plural has one extra quirk: the noun itself adds **-n** if it doesn't already end in -n. *die Zimmer → in den Zimmer**n***, *die Kinder → mit den Kinder**n***.
Possessives follow the *ein* pattern: *meinem*, *meiner*, *meinem*, *meinen*. *Ich wohne bei **meiner** Schwester.*

grammars.title: Place prepositions: staying put or moving?
body: The nine prepositions below take the **Dativ** when they answer *wo?* (where — no movement) and the **Akkusativ** when they answer *wohin?* (where to — movement). In this unit you'll use the first.
after: How to decide in one second: **if the thing moves from one place to another, use the Akkusativ; if not, use the Dativ.** *Das Buch liegt auf **dem** Tisch* (staying put) but *Ich lege das Buch auf **den** Tisch* (moving there).
For now, just master the Dativ side — that's what you need to describe a room. The Akkusativ side will come naturally once you start talking about going places in unit 14.

head: German
English
rows: The bed is in the bedroom.
Der Fernseher steht auf dem Regal.
The TV is on the shelf.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch.
The book is on the table.
Das Bild hängt über dem Sofa.
The picture is above the sofa.
Die Schuhe stehen unter dem Bett.
The shoes are under the bed.
Das Bad ist neben der Küche.
The bathroom is next to the kitchen.
Der Garten ist hinter dem Haus.
The garden is behind the house.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Watch the verbs: *stehen* for things standing upright, *liegen* for things lying flat, *hängen* for things hanging. Using *sein* for all of them isn't wrong, but it instantly sounds like a translated textbook.
Rental ads in Germany are written in dense abbreviations. Recognizing the ten below makes half of any ad readable right away.

blocks.title: Describing your own home
items: *Ich wohne in einer Wohnung / in einem Haus / in einem Zimmer.*
*Die Wohnung hat … Zimmer. Es gibt auch einen Balkon / einen Garten.*
*Ich wohne allein / mit meiner Familie / mit Freunden.*

blocks.text: Those four sentences are a complete answer to *Wie wohnst du?*, one of the questions most certain to come up in the A1 speaking exam — and in your first conversation with a new neighbor.

items: Es gibt ein Schlafzimmer und ein Wohnzimmer.
Der Fernseher steht auf dem Regal.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right Dativ article: *dem* or *der*.
Put the words in the right order.
items: auf dem Tisch / das Buch / liegt
in einer Wohnung / ich / wohne / allein

answers: There's a bedroom and a living room. — Where's the bathroom? — Next to the kitchen, at the back on the right. — The TV is on the shelf. — My bed is in the bedroom. — How much is the rent?
der — dem — dem — dem — dem — dem
Es gibt einen Balkon. — Wo ist das Bad? — Mein Bett steht im Schlafzimmer. — Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. — Wie hoch ist die Miete? — Ich wohne allein in einer Wohnung.
